articles.title: Uttam Kumar birth centenary; PM Narendra Modi pays tribute to Bengali cinema's 'Mahanayak'; recalls Satyajit Ray's 'Nayak' connection
articles.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi paid tribute to legendary Bengali actor Uttam Kumar in the 137th episode of 'Mann Ki Baat', ahead of the actor's birth ce.
articles.body: Prime Minister Narendra Modi paid tribute to legendary Bengali actor Uttam Kumar in the 137th episode of 'Mann Ki Baat', ahead of the actor's birth centenary on September 3.PM Modi described Kumar as a versatile performer who captivated audiences and earned a lasting place in their hearts."On September 3, we will mark the birth centenary of legendary actor Uttam Kumar. A versatile performer, he captivated audiences with his remarkable portrayals and earned a lasting place in the hearts of people," the Prime Minister said.Born Arun Kumar Chattopadhyay on September 3, 1926, Uttam Kumar is fondly remembered as "Mahanayak" of Bengali cinema. His career spanned more than three decades, during which he worked as an actor, director, producer, screenwriter and composer.In his address, PM Modi also referred to the enduring connection between Uttam Kumar and filmmaker Satyajit Ray. Film lovers have long believed that Ray wrote his 1966 film 'Nayak- The Hero' with Uttam Kumar in mind."Uttam Kumar ji was a versatile actor who won hearts with his acting. Film lovers believe that Mr Satyajit Ray wrote the entire script of the film 'Nayak-The Hero' keeping the great hero Uttam Kumar ji in mind. Mr Satyajit Ray had said that he had dignity along with amazing emotional depth. He worked very hard to bring the character to life," Modi said.Uttam Kumar's portrayal of the complex matinee idol in 'Nayak' remains one of the defining performances of his career.The film explored the psychological pressures surrounding fame, with Kumar bringing vulnerability and emotional depth to the central character.The actor's rise to stardom followed a difficult beginning. His film journey started with a supporting role in 'Drishtidan' in 1948, while his early releases faced repeated box-office failures. He eventually found success with 'Basu Paribar' in 1952.The 1953 film 'Sharey Chuattor' marked a major turning point and also established his celebrated screen partnership with Suchitra Sen. The duo went on to feature together in several popular films, including 'Agni Pariksha', 'Harano Sur' and 'Saptapadi.'Uttam Kumar also achieved a significant milestone when he became the first recipient of the National Film Award for Best Actor in 1967, recognised for his performances in 'Antony Firingee' and Satyajit Ray's 'Chiriyakhana.'Beyond acting, Kumar directed films, composed music and sang playback tracks. He was also known for his philanthropy and resilience, with his contributions extending beyond cinema.Uttam Kumar died following a heart attack on July 24, 1980. His legacy continues to occupy a central place in Bengali cinema.Give your child the gift of confidence! Claim your exclusive TOI Masterclass spot today!

articles.title: Man killed at Big Church Festival named as his church leads tributes
articles.summary: Robert Guanco, 41, was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.
articles.body:
The man killed at a Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday has been named by his church as Robert Guanco, 41.

He was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.

Six other people were injured at the event by a falling sign at the Big Church Festival , near Steyning, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment.

In a statement, his church said: "Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love, and his service to God will never be forgotten."

The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.

The festival, at Wiston Park, began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.

The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.

Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them.

"And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events."

articles.title: ‘Toxic’ box office collection Day 5 [LIVE]: Yash and Kiara Advani film eyes Rs 204 crore India net milestone
articles.summary: Yash’s much-anticipated gangster actioner ‘Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups’, directed by Geetu Mohandas, is currently in its first Sunday at the box.
articles.body: Yash’s much-anticipated gangster actioner ‘Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups’, directed by Geetu Mohandas, is currently in its first Sunday at the box office. After opening to a massive Rs 101.10 crore net in India, the film has maintained a steady run through its first weekend.After collecting Rs 37.65 crore on Day 2, Rs 27.20 crore on Day 3 and Rs 25.15 crore on Day 4, the Yash starrer is now inching closer to the Rs 200 crore mark in India net collections. As the weekend comes to a close, all eyes are on whether ‘Toxic’ can maintain its momentum on Sunday.According to the latest figures, ‘Toxic’ has already crossed Rs 255 crore in worldwide gross collections, while its India net collection is nearing the Rs 200 crore milestone. The film’s performance over the next few hours will offer a clearer picture of its first-weekend run.Toxic Movie Review‘Toxic’ Day 1 to Day 4 collections‘Toxic’ opened with a massive Rs 101.10 crore net in India on Day 1 from 24,579 shows. On Day 2, the film added Rs 37.65 crore net from 22,629 shows, taking its India net collection to Rs 138.75 crore, while its domestic gross stood at Rs 165.85 crore. articles.title: Antonio Maestre lanza un pronóstico de las futuras elecciones en España: “Uno de cada cuatro jóvenes votaría a la extrema derecha”
articles.standfirst: El periodista ha explicado en La Sexta por qué la balanza se inclina hacia este lado
articles.summary: El periodista ha explicado en La Sexta por qué la balanza se inclina hacia este lado
articles.body: Antonio Maestre ha explicado en el plató de ‘La Sexta Xplica’ por qué el número de jóvenes que votan a la derecha va en aumento. “Uno de cada cuatro jóvenes va a votar a Vox”, argumenta. “Un 23% de los jóvenes votarían a la extrema derecha, lo que significa que un 77%, no. Por lo tanto, hay una inmensa mayoría de jóvenes que no lo haría”, explica Maestre. Si bien, asegura que, a pesar de estos datos, la balanza comienza a coger peso del lado derecho: “Sí que es cierto que ha habido un deslizamiento entre bloques hacia la extrema derecha de las personas que antes igual eran más conservadoras, pero éstas no son la inmensa mayoría”, añade. En su intervención en el programa de La Sexta, Maestre compara las generaciones jóvenes de derecha con las de la izquierda: “Más quisiera la extrema derecha convocar manifestaciones tan masivas como las que convoca, por ejemplo, la organizadora juvenil socialista, en muchos lugares de España y tampoco decimos que la juventud se ha hecho comunista”. “Algunos datos dicen que hay más porcentaje de jóvenes votantes al PSOE que a VOX y no decimos que los jóvenes son ‘sociatas”. Para Maestre, el que, a pesar de haber más jóvenes de izquierdas, aumente el número de votantes jóvenes de derecha es consecuencia de varios factores: “Si se ha dado este deslizamiento hacia la extrema derecha es porque, primero, hay una polarización en la sociedad y segundo porque ha habido 8 años de gobierno de izquierdas”. No es la primera vez que Maestre aborda el tema del voto joven en ‘LaSexta Xplica’. En noviembre aseguró que esta tendencia hacia la extrema derecha ya se daba y que la mayoría eran varones. "Lo que está ocurriendo en la actualidad es que hay una base de jóvenes conservadores que durante muchísimo tiempo habían tenido un mínimo de vergüenza a la hora de defender ciertos postulados de defensa de la dictadura y que ahora, como existe un partido como Vox, se han sentido legitimados para poder defender lo que antes hacían en privado y ahora hacerlo de manera pública", detalla. Además, ha subrayado que "existe un corrimiento conservador de los varones jóvenes".

articles.title: Dulquer Salmaan was almost launched with ‘Ritu’ before ‘Second Show’, Shyamaprasad reveals how actor’s debut plan fell through
articles.summary: Dulquer Salmaan has built a career that stands firmly on his own, moving beyond the shadow of his superstar father Mammootty to become one of Malayala.
articles.body: Dulquer Salmaan has built a career that stands firmly on his own, moving beyond the shadow of his superstar father Mammootty to become one of Malayalam cinema’s most recognisable names across India. However, his acting journey could have started several years earlier than it eventually did.As Dulquer prepares for the worldwide release of his upcoming film ‘I’m Game’, a revelation by filmmaker Shyamaprasad has brought an interesting piece of the actor’s early career back into focus. The director disclosed that Dulquer was once considered for his 2009 film ‘Ritu’, a project that played an important role in the changing landscape of Malayalam cinema.Dulquer’s debut could have happened before Second ShowDulquer eventually made his acting debut with Srinath Rajendran’s ‘Second Show’ in 2012. The gangster drama did not follow the conventional template of a commercial action film and was among the movies associated with the emerging new-generation wave in Malayalam cinema.However, according to Shyamaprasad, the actor was initially expected to enter the industry through ‘Ritu’, which arrived three years before ‘Second Show’. The film was among a group of Malayalam movies that helped introduce a different style of storytelling and contributed to the transformation that eventually became more prominent with films such as ‘Traffic’.Shyamaprasad recalls meeting young DulquerAccording To SCREEN, speaking at the pre-release event of ‘I’m Game’, Shyamaprasad remembered his connection with Dulquer from the time he was working with Mammootty on ‘Ore Kadal’.“I’ve known Dulquer for a long time. When I was shooting Ore Kadal (2007) with Mammootty in Chennai, Dulquer was young, and he used to come play cricket nearby. I was supposed to cast him in my film Ritu. It was almost there, but it didn’t happen, unfortunately.”‘Ritu’ eventually introduced audiences to several young performers, including Asif Ali, Rima Kallingal, Nishan and Vinay Forrt, many of whom went on to establish themselves in Malayalam cinema.Why Dulquer chose I’m GameMore than a decade into his career, Dulquer is now approaching his 40th film as a lead actor with ‘I’m Game’. At the film’s pre-release event, he explained that his approach to selecting roles has changed, particularly when a script pushes him beyond his comfort zone.“Some time back, I made a decision that I would attempt roles I am most afraid of from now on. If it feels familiar, I might take it lightly. Now, when I hear a script and it makes me think, ‘How will I do this?’ I take it on. When I heard I’m Game’s narration, I got scared, thinking about how I would pull it off.”The actor also credited Antony Varghese Pepe for playing a crucial role in the project and described him as “the true hero of I’m Game.”“He is like my brother and came to work in the movie as soon as I called,” Dulquer said.Dulquer praises Kayadu Lohar and Nahas HidhayathDulquer also had words of appreciation for Kayadu Lohar, who is part of the film’s cast. He highlighted her acting abilities while discussing the challenges that can come with being perceived primarily for one’s appearance.“We call Kayadu ‘Dudu’ because we didn’t know how to pronounce her name correctly. As Mysskin sir said, being pretty might be a disadvantage for her, as people might think she’s too pretty for roles. But she is a strong performer as well.”The actor described director Nahas Hidhayath’s film as his “most ambitious film” and revealed that it was the filmmaker’s first script.“This film is an absolute Onasadya (Onam feast). It has all the ingredients. He’s cooked it with great effort.”Dulquer Salmaan’s next releaseDirected by Nahas Hidhayath, ‘I’m Game’ is an action thriller that brings together Dulquer Salmaan, Antony Varghese Pepe and Kayadu Lohar. The film is being positioned as an ambitious project for the director and marks another challenging role for Dulquer.‘I’m Game’ is scheduled to release worldwide on September 3, 2026. articles.title: Jimi Hendrix’s final words to roadie revealed after violent Hells Angels clash
articles.summary: Eric Barrett recalls Jimi Hendrix's final concert at the Isle of Fehmarn, where Hells Angels violence forced a harrowing escape before his death.
articles.body: It was supposed to be another stop on the road for Jimi Hendrix — but a festival marred by violence and chaos would become the rock legend's final official concert performance. Eric Barrett, who was Hendrix's roadie and confidant from 1968 to 1970, has written a memoir, "Experienced: On the Road with Jimi Hendrix and Beyond." Barrett went on to spend nearly five decades working behind the scenes with other iconic artists, including Madonna, David Bowie and Aerosmith. "We were playing on the Isle of Fehmarn, and the Hells Angels had taken over," Barrett recalled to Fox News Digital. "There was no control. It was a scary place to be. We had two cars there waiting to get us off the island and go back to London. But the Hells Angels didn't want us to get off the island. They wanted the boys to stay and party. And then it got violent." PAUL MCCARTNEY REVEALS HOW A 'HAPPY' TEEN HITCHHIKING TRIP WITH GEORGE HARRISON DELIVERED A SHOCK According to Barrett's book, hundreds of Hells Angels descended on the island and took over the venue. He wrote that many fans who had been camping out were "beaten and robbed" as festival security was chased off. Hendrix, he said, took one look at the mayhem and retreated to his room "alone, sober." The outlaw motorcycle club had taken over. The next day, Hendrix took the stage and was met with boos. He told the hostile audience, "I don't give a f--- if you boo, as long as you boo in key, you mothers," before chuckling. When he was done, Hendrix told the audience, "Thank you, goodbye. Peace!" Barrett ushered Hendrix and the band off the stage toward the waiting cars. Barrett was eager to get out. But then the bikers surrounded them. WATCH: CARLOS SANTANA RECALLS THE MOMENT HE IMPRESSED JIMI HENDRIX: ‘I’LL TAKE IT’ "I saw a Hells Angel about to hit [tour manager] Gerry Stickells over the head with this baton," said Barrett. "I put my arm up to take the blow. I nearly passed out from the pain, but imagine if it had landed on Gerry's skull? We managed to get inside the car. Jimi kept looking at me because he saw me take the blow. He just said to me, 'Are you OK, Eric? Are you OK?' He kept asking me if I was OK. That's just the kind of man he was. And... that was the last thing he ever said to me." On Sept. 18, 1970, paramedics arrived at Monika Dannemann's apartment at the Samarkand Hotel in London and found Hendrix unresponsive. He was 27. Stickells broke the news to Barrett. "I couldn't believe it," said Barrett. "I remember walking around London in a fog. It was a stupid, tragic accident. He took too many of [girlfriend] Monika Dannemann's sleeping pills. She supposedly had these incredibly powerful German tranquilizers. And she said he took nine of them. She couldn't wake him. She called Eric Burdon of The Animals, who was a good friend of Jimi's. He screamed at her, 'Call the f-----g ambulance!'" "What I'm being told was the ambulance guys ... laid him on his back, and he threw up," said Barrett. "He asphyxiated. That was the accident. The pills were the accident. Tragedy was him dying." In the book, Barrett wrote, "The paramedics arrived but couldn't revive Jimi. They carried him out on a stretcher to the ambulance, assuring Monika that he was going to be all right. Either lying in bed on his back or on the way to the hospital, Jimi threw up on himself. The post-mortem concluded that Jimi had died of asphyxia while intoxicated with barbiturates." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "... I flashed back to the time I took too much Mandrax, and my girlfriend couldn't wake me up," he wrote. "It was easily done and could've happened to any of us in Jimi's group of friends. That it happened to Jimi himself was heartbreaking. But I've never heard anything to make me think Jimi's death was anything other than what it appeared." Barrett firmly rejected the rumors and conspiracy theories that have surrounded Hendrix's death for decades. Among them was an allegation by former roadie James "Tappy" Wright, who wrote in his 2009 memoir, "Rock Roadie," that Hendrix’s manager, Mike Jeffery, confessed to killing Hendrix, The Guardian reported. Barrett strongly disputes Wright's account and rejects any suggestion that Hendrix was murdered. "I don't believe for a second that Mike Jeffery was the cause of Jimi's death," he said. "I just don't believe it. The circumstances don't add up. And I was told by so many people that Tappy only wrote that to try and sell books. But I've never believed it. I will never believe it. I was there, and right now I'm probably the last man standing. All the lads are passing. So no, I wouldn't believe that for a second." Jeffery died in a plane crash near Nantes, France, in 1973. Dannemann died in an apparent suicide in 1996, two days after she was found guilty of contempt of court in a long-running legal dispute with Kathy Etchingham, another former girlfriend of Hendrix's. She was 50. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS Barrett said that shortly after Hendrix's death, he lied to reporters about Hendrix's drug use. "I was, what, 24 when he passed?" said Barrett. "I didn't want to besmirch his memory. So I lied. I just wanted people to see him in a good light. But I came to realize as I got older that I didn't have to lie. Yes, he took drugs. Did he take heroin? I've never seen heroin anywhere near him. I've worked on many backstages for almost 50 years. I know it's a drug that has killed a lot of musicians. But I don't believe Jimi was taking it. He smoked pot. He took a lot of LSD. He took pills. But I don't believe he was into heroin." Looking back, Barrett described Hendrix as "a wild man" on stage. The musician was famous for playing the guitar behind his head and with his teeth. He would also smash guitars and amps during encores and, on occasion, set his guitar on fire. But when the shows were over and audiences had long since left, Hendrix was a "quiet, mild-mannered, polite young man." "He talked to everyone," he said. "He was very charming. And he was shy. People were in awe of Jimi. And when he had his guitar around his neck, over his shoulder, he was comfortable. That was his crutch. But I also remember Paul McCartney walking towards him, and he's gasping, 'It's Paul McCartney!' He was just a shy man who didn't know how to take the accolades of his talent." "I have so many memories of that wonderful man," Barrett continued. "I remember we were all staying in Benedict Canyon and it was my birthday. We were all hanging out by the pool, and Jimi came out in no shirt, just velvet pants. He goes, 'Eric, Eric!' I responded, 'Hey Jimi, what do you need?' He smiled and went, 'Happy birthday, man. Here's some money. Go and buy yourself something you really want.' He gave me $500, which was a huge amount back then." "I went to North Beach Leathers, a place I'd seen Jimi had bought some clothes from. I bought myself this long leather coat, spent all my money on it. It was the best gift I ever bought. When I came back, he loved it. He went, 'Wow, that's a coat! I wish I had seen that before you.'" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I was on a plane with him after a show," he said. "Jimi looked at me and said, 'Eric, what do you think, will they remember me?' I was flabbergasted. I went, 'Will they remember you? You're huge over here.' But he was so insecure. 'Are you sure, Eric? What if the kids don't come?' I just told him, 'When it comes to success, you have nothing to worry about.' That was Jimi, a gift to the Earth from the Lord. And I miss him."

articles.title: 'Hercules' star Kevin Sorbo says California can keep its taxes, traffic and 'negativity': 'I'm done'
articles.summary: "Elijah Peel" actor Kevin Sorbo says California can keep its taxes, traffic, and "negativity" after moving to Florida nearly seven years ago for his family and career.
articles.body: Kevin Sorbo has officially closed the door on California. Nearly seven years after leaving the Golden State for Florida, the "Hercules" star says he has no interest in going back — and he's got three reasons why: "Taxes, traffic and negativity." In an interview with Fox News Digital, Sorbo, who stars in the faith-based movie "Elijah Peel," said his move to Florida has given him something he felt was increasingly difficult to find in California — "acceptance." articles.title: Dolly Parton's most iconic 'Dolly-isms' on beauty, wigs, Botox and living life on her own terms
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's iconic one-liners about her wigs, rhinestone outfits and cosmetic procedures captured her philosophy on authenticity and confidence.
articles.body: Dolly Parton died peacefully in Nashville after a brief battle with cancer on Tuesday. The country music icon was 80 and spent decades in the limelight. Along with her beloved music and philanthropic works, Parton will be remembered by fans for the many "Dolly-isms" she's shared over the years. In 2022, the "9 to 5" singer herself took to Instagram to share some of her favorite quotes she's given. In the video, she also gave a "translation" of what some of her famous one-liners meant. For example, she once said, "It’s hard to be a diamond in a rhinestone world," which she explained meant, "Why blend in when standing out is so much more fun!" Another famous line she included was, "It costs a lot of money to look this cheap," which she translated to, "All that matters is being yourself and feeling great about it." Below is a look at the most famous "Dolly-isms" over the years. DOLLY PARTON SLEPT AS LITTLE AS 3 HOURS, DID HER OWN HAIR AND MAKEUP ON SET, CO-STAR DANICA MCKELLAR SAYS 'It costs a lot of money to look this cheap.' Parton has said this line several times, describing her over-the-top and glamorous appearance. In 2017, she repeated the line to Vogue, describing her approach to make-up. 'I’m not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I’m not dumb — and I’m not blonde either.' This is another popular line Parton used throughout her career. During the same Vogue interview, the "Jolene" singer repeated the line when discussing her wig collection. 'People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don’t know, I’m never there.' During the same Vogue interview in 2017, Parton gave this quote, explaining that she turned to using wigs to create her signature hairstyle. 'I am a self-made woman, and I have the doctor bills to prove it.' The exact time and place Parton gave this famous line about her cosmetics procedures is not recorded, but the line has been famously quoted for years. 'Find out who you are and do it on purpose.' During Parton's 2009 University of Tennessee commencement speech, the legend gave this quote to the graduating class. 'The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain.' This is one of Parton's most famous mantras that she repeated over the years. She also posted the quote on her X account in 2013. 'If you see someone without a smile today, give ’em yours.' Parton famously shared this quote over the years, spreading her positivity and encouraging others to do the same. In 2019, she shared the line on social media, alongside a throwback photo of herself, and included the hashtag "Monday Motivation." 'I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond.' Parton gave this quote during an interview with Elle in 2019. This line came after she recalled the moment her friend and mentor, country star Chet Atkins, advised her to "tone it down" early on in her career. She remembered Atkins telling her she wouldn't be taken seriously in the industry if she continued wearing rhinestone outfits and getting cosmetic procedures done. 'I’m not going to limit myself just because people won’t accept the fact that I can do something else.' In November 2010, Parton took to X to share her own philosophy about how she lived her life. The quote summed up her refusal to stay only a country singer as she built a career in film, business and philanthropy. You don’t have to be a raving beauty to be special and to be beautiful.' In 2018, Parton and Jennifer Aniston sat down for an interview with "Good Morning America" to promote their movie "Dumplin'." 'People say I look so happy — and I say, ‘That’s the Botox.' During Parton's Vogue feature in 2017, the country star joked about the cosmetic procedures that she'd had done, including Botox. 'I never think of myself as a star because, as somebody once said, ‘A star is nothing but a big ball of gas’ — and I don’t want to be that.' During an interview with Billboard in 2014, Parton shared that she was "just a working girl" and used her comedic personality to put a spin on how she didn't view herself as a huge star.
